\chapter{Parts of a House}
\label{ch:sa-parts-of-a-house}
\hlchaptermodality{47}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name a wall, a window, a stair, a pillar and the floor in Sanskrit.}

Complete SA-C47-floor and demonstrate the chapter promise.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[bhittiḥ]{\sk{भित्तिः} (bhittiḥ) — a wall}

\label{lesson:SA-C47-wall}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{tāpaḥ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{भित्तिः}}
\textbf{\sk{भित्तिः}} (\emph{bhittiḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a wall\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{भित्तिः}} is a wall: the built side of a room.

You know \sk{पुरम्}, the town with a wall around it. \textbf{\sk{भित्तिः}} is one such wall brought down to the size of a house — the thing itself rather than the place it encloses.

It stands on \emph{bhid}, \textquotedblleft{}to split, to break apart\textquotedblright{}, which is exactly what a wall does to a space: inside on one hand, outside on the other. Latin \emph{findere}, \textquotedblleft{}to cleave\textquotedblright{}, is the same root, behind English \emph{fissure}, and English \emph{bite} belongs to it as well.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One wall, told apart from the walled town.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bhittiḥ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{tāpaḥ}, then \emph{bhittiḥ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{भित्तिः} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a wall\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vātāyanam]{\sk{वातायनम्} (vātāyanam) — a window}

\label{lesson:SA-C47-window}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{bhittiḥ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{वातायनम्}}
\textbf{\sk{वातायनम्}} (\emph{vātāyanam}) — \textquotedblleft{}a window\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{वातायनम्}} is a window, and the word says plainly what a window is for.

It is \emph{vāta}, wind, joined to \emph{ayana}, a going: a window is the wind's way in. You already say \sk{वायुः} for wind, and \emph{vāta} is its near relative from the same root, \textquotedblleft{}to blow\textquotedblright{}.

Set it against \sk{भित्तिः} and the pair makes sense of a room: the wall shuts, the window opens. Neuter, ending in \textbf{-\sk{अम्}}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The opening in the wall, named for what comes through it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vātāyanam}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{bhittiḥ}, then \emph{vātāyanam}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{वातायनम्} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a window\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sopānam]{\sk{सोपानम्} (sopānam) — a stair}

\label{lesson:SA-C47-stair}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{vātāyanam} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{सोपानम्}}
\textbf{\sk{सोपानम्}} (\emph{sopānam}) — \textquotedblleft{}a stair\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{सोपानम्}} is a stair, a flight of steps.

The usual way of taking it apart reads it as \textquotedblleft{}the means of going up\textquotedblright{} — a small joining word in front, and behind it the sense of rising. The word carries its purpose on its face, the way \sk{वातायनम्} does.

It stayed home and stayed itself: Hindi and Marathi both keep \emph{sopān} for a stair. Neuter, ending in \textbf{-\sk{अम्}}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The way up, added to the wall and the window.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sopānam}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{vātāyanam}, then \emph{sopānam}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{सोपानम्} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a stair\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[stambhaḥ]{\sk{स्तम्भः} (stambhaḥ) — a pillar}

\label{lesson:SA-C47-pillar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{sopānam} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{स्तम्भः}}
\textbf{\sk{स्तम्भः}} (\emph{stambhaḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a pillar\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{स्तम्भः}} is a pillar, a post: the upright that carries a roof.

It rests on \emph{stambh}, \textquotedblleft{}to prop, to make firm\textquotedblright{}. Where \sk{भित्तिः} splits a space, \textbf{\sk{स्तम्भः}} holds one open — a wall you can walk past.

English \emph{staff} and \emph{stamp} sit near it, and the picture under all three is one thing: something planted hard and standing. Ends in \textbf{-\sk{अः}}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
What holds the roof up, beside what closes the room in.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{stambhaḥ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{sopānam}, then \emph{stambhaḥ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{स्तम्भः} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a pillar\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[talam]{\sk{तलम्} (talam) — the floor}

\label{lesson:SA-C47-floor}



\begin{quote}
Before the last word of the chapter: what did \emph{sopānam} mean, and what did \emph{stambhaḥ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{तलम्}}
\textbf{\sk{तलम्}} (\emph{talam}) — \textquotedblleft{}the floor\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{तलम्}} is the floor: the flat under a room, and the underside of anything at all.

The palm of a hand is a \emph{tala}, and so is the sole of a foot. The word names a flat bottom rather than a room in particular, which is why it reaches from a building to a body without changing shape.

Latin \emph{tellūs}, \textquotedblleft{}the ground\textquotedblright{}, is a cousin of it. Neuter, ending in \textbf{-\sk{अम्}}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five parts of a building: a wall, a window, a stair, a pillar, the floor.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{talam}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then \emph{bhittiḥ} and \emph{talam} together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{तलम्} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}the floor\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
